source_row.wylie: dang po ni, srog gcod pa gang zhe na, 'di la bsdu bar gzhi dang 'du shes dang bsam pa dang nyon mongs dang mtha' ste lngar gsungs kyang , bar pa gsum bsam par bsdus te sbyor ba bsnan nas gzhi dang bsam pa dang sbyor ba dang mthar thug bzhi bzhir bsdus te bshad na 'jug pa bde zhing dgongs pa dang mi 'gal lo,
source_row.english: Here is the first. One may ask, "How do you define the act of killing?" The Abbreviation says that five parts are involved: the object, the conception, the thinking, the bad thought, and the conclusion. These five can be shortened into four: the middle three can be included into the thinking, and we can add the stage of undertaking; this makes the presentation easier, and in no way violates the intention of the original text.

The complete killing compound supplies the single English word killing. There is no independent life word for a SROG member, and GCOD is not split into a degenerate member covering the whole English parent.
The question-introducing formula owns ask. One may and the definition question content remain outside this narrow formula.
The complete inflected title form refers to the work named Abbreviation. Full BSDU BA records support that title; preserve the final R rather than cutting BAR into BA plus a suffix.
First GZHI names the object in the initial five-part list. The later repeated GZHI is not assigned this same word.
The complete cognition/conception term names the second part, not an English thinking repetition.
First BSAM PA names the third part in the initial five-part list.
The complete afflictive-state term is rendered bad thought here. Its whole lexical evidence supports this established translation; no separate NYON or MONGS members are invented.
This last DANG in the five-part list has the explicit final and. Earlier serial conjunctions are not copied onto it.
First conclusion term is the end of the five-part list. It is distinct from later MTHAR THUG in the condensed four-part Tibetan list.
The complete inflected numeral owns the first five, preserving its final R. The later English These five is an anaphoric repetition and receives no second claim.
The saying verb introduces the cited classification. Exclude supplied that and parts are involved.
The middle subset comprises conception, thinking and bad thought. Middle belongs with three, not with the first or final numbers.
The cardinal counts those middle three components.
The complete inflected BSAM PAR supplies the second thinking, the category into which the middle three are included. Retain PAR whole; no detached R claim.
This first BSDUS is the inclusion of the middle three into thinking. The later final BSDUS is represented separately by shortened in the English overview.
This connective joins the inclusion and adding-undertaking operations. The exact and before we can add is distinct from the initial list conjunction and the closing coordination.
First undertaking noun names the newly added stage. Stage of is English explanatory wording and stays outside.
The adding verb owns add in the four-part restructuring. Supplied we can remains outside.

The complete repeated distributive numeral phrase describes arrangement into four. English states that result once; the whole phrase avoids inventing a second four or treating the repetition as an absence null.
Final BSDUS is the overall condensation into four, recast earlier in English as shortened. Source order and English order differ; this is not the first BSDUS/included occurrence.
The explanation/exposition sense is rendered by the noun presentation. The source conditional and ease-of-engagement construction is recast around it; this narrow noun excludes this makes and easier.
The ease word supplies easier, with an ordinary comparative form. The preceding engagement verb is not independently mapped to the same word.
The connective coordinates ease of presentation with consistency with the text intention. It owns this final and, not either earlier list/operation connector.
The complete intention term owns intention. Of the original text supplies the referent explicitly in English and remains outside this noun.
Standalone negation is realized by the complete negative phrase in no way. Exclude violates, which belongs to the following lexical verb.
The contravene/conflict verb is rendered violates. The following LO remains a separate terminal marker, not part of the lexical verb.

spans.nul: The terminal LO closes the completed statement after MI ’GAL. English closes the same statement with its final period; there is no additional lexical English word for this closure. This is affirmative punctuation fusion, not an uncertain lexical omission.

None is converted to an absence null.
